props.title: La Chinoise

sections.content: La Chinoise marks Jean-Luc Godard's radical shift from playful New Wave experimentation to militant political cinema. Shot in vivid primary colors that echo Maoist propaganda, the film follows five young Parisian students forming a Marxist-Leninist cell in a borrowed apartment. Godard's fragmented narrative style reaches new heights here, mixing direct-to-camera monologues, theatrical staging, and documentary-like sequences. The film eerily predicted the May 1968 student protests in France, coming just months before the actual events. Like Weekend (1967) from the same year, it shows Godard's increasing disillusionment with traditional narrative cinema.

sections.content: The influence of La Chinoise reverberates through political cinema of the late 1960s and 1970s. Bernardo Bertolucci's The Dreamers (2003) directly references it during the Paris sequences, while Medium Cool (1969) adopts its pseudo-documentary style to capture real protests at the 1968 Democratic Convention. The film's technique of having actors break character to discuss politics influenced later works like Punishment Park (1971) and Jean-Marie Straub's Not Reconciled (1965). SUBHEAD: Revolutionary Cinema & Political Modernism

Godard's use of Brechtian distancing techniques reached their apex in La Chinoise, inspiring a wave of experimental political films. The direct address to camera would influence Battle of Algiers (1966) and Costa-Gavras's Z (1969). The film's bold use of color coding (particularly red) and revolutionary iconography can be seen in later works like Investigation of a Citizen Above Suspicion (1970) and Nagisa Oshima's The Man Who Left His Will on Film (1970).
